newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Century Group seeks international stardom.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Century Group seeks international stardom.

text.p: When businessman Omar Salah started wooing foreign partners to Jordan two years ago, rivals scoffed at his plans to produce Jordanian goods that could compete in the global market.

But Salah's pioneering Century Group, a conglomerate of joint ventures ranging from software to sand mining, has defied the doubters. It aims to be Jordan's top textile exporter in 1997, with more ambitious projects coming onstream within two years.
Its clothes, supplied to major retailers, are already on sale in top stores throughout Europe and the United States.

"Any shopping mall in the United States, in the biggest stores, you will find one of our products. We sell to The Gap, Victoria's Secret, Polo Ralph Lauren, Structure, to J. Crew and Banana Republic," said Salah, 30.
"It was not an easy thing from the beginning, because the ideas I had required markets that Jordan did not have."
While Jordan's business hopes were mostly dashed by the modest trickle of foreign capital since its 1994 peace treaty with Israel, Century found ways to reap the "peace dividend."
Salah's secret was to attract multinationals as 50 percent equity partners to Jordan. Century could produce brand-name goods in Jordan, which were presold to Western markets.
The firm, employing 1,000 people since it was set up in 1995, aims to be Jordan's largest industrial conglomerate by 2000.
Century also caught the attention of emerging funds looking at regional opportunities, including ING Baring's, whose Middle East director, Angus Blair, rates it highly for his clients.

"It's amazing for someone of his age ... who is not just looking at creating a profitable business but employing people and creating competitive business which Jordan is benefiting enormously from," Blair said of Salah. "He's unique."
Century has already lined up 12 projects, with a total of $100 million of investments, half of which are now in operation. The rest are due by the end of 1998 or early 1999.
Its partners include Sara Lee Corp. and Levi Strauss & Co. in textiles; and Motorola Inc. in software. It has also joined with other companies in plastics ventures, sand mining and retailing.

Three industrial projects with Dutch firms came on stream in 1997 -- the largest an $8 million can-making plant with Dutch Can Pack producing 350 million cans annually and a $1 million dairy pudding plant with Balton. The third with Antilles Gold is in jewellery casting.
A $5 million mining project with Belgium's Sibelco to export silica for glassware should be ready by September and another with Motorola to develop software is being negotiated.
A pioneering $2 million project to produce medical textiles such as hospital sheets with Cincinnati-based American Standard Textiles for the European market should be ready by end of 1977.
"Right now they are sewing in the U.S. and exporting to Europe. They decided instead Jordan will sew medical textiles and re-export to Europe and save a lot of money," Salah said.

Century's first three $10 million ventures with Sara Lee have a $60 million sales target by end of 1997, which would make it the country's largest textile exporter. A new $3 million Levi's plant to produce shirts is due for the end of 1997.

Forging strong ties with U.S. retailers, Century plans a $24 million shopping mall to be opened in Jordan by 1999. It has also set up Jordan's first buying office with the German mail order group Otto Reichelt AG to act as a channel to "help Jordanian firms export all over the world," Salah said.
Century has also found a niche in attracting U.S. and European multinationals established in Israel who have either downsized or shifted some of their plants to Jordan.

"A lot of European and American investors who traditionally had long-term investments in Israel now see they have no longer competitive wages in Israel and decided to shut down their plants and start new plants in Jordan," Salah said.
In the span of less than a year, Century has become the biggest investor in the Irbid industrial estate, only an hour's drive away from Israel's northern industrial heartland.

Production costs between 40 and 70 percent lower than in Israel have been a major incentive for global giants such as Sara Lee, already located in Israel, who eye expansion in both the Israeli and European markets from its plant in Jordan.
"We knew the secret to marketing is to do a joint venture where your partner assures you of a market ... We wanted to guarantee the market from the start," Salah said.
A pool of competitive and educated workers, along with Jordan's close proximity to Europe, gives the country an advantage as a potential outsourcing site for multinationals.
"Jordan has access to markets around the world and we have very competitive labour and it's getting better," Salah said.
